ch10 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that a serialized zombie apocalypse, unlike a zombie movie, lets us explore life among the dead: how survivors like Rick, Lori, and Glenn should treat one another and divide labor, whether private property and equality survive without government, invoking Morgan weighing photo albums against supplies and the question of whether the new world is 'nasty, brutish, and short'. It frames zombies philosophically through Descartes's mindless automatons and Chalmers's P-zombies, and asks whether killing a walker could be wrong if walkers have inner lives, like dolphins or pandas, just less cute.

chapters.file: ch11 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
ch12 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.

chapters.file: ch13 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether you survive a walker bite, rejecting the body view via Dr. Jenner's 'Everything you ever were or ever will be—gone' because a mindless corpse is not you. He tests philosophical behaviorism and functionalism against walker behavior—Jenny turning her old doorknob, walkers distinguishing humans by smell—then adapts Dennett's thought experiment into a walker-and-rope computer functionally identical to a human brain. Since we can conceive that groaning machine lacking inner experience, behavior and function cannot settle which systems are conscious, leaving the bitten dying in ignorance of whether they face annihilation or reanimation.

chapters.file: ch14 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Richard Greene surveys zombie types, from the radio-using corpse of Return of the Living Dead to White Zombie's servants, to fix walkers as the standard zombie worth asking what they know. Against Dr. Jenner's 'mindless instinct' verdict he cites the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, Jenny working her former home's doorknob, walkers breaking a shop window with a rock, and their sniffing out Rick and Glenn's gut disguise as evidence of genuine beliefs. He argues that zombie knowledge, which cannot involve weighing evidence, supports externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge over internalist ones, and that walkers know only simple things recalled from past experience—the more complex the task, the less likely they know it.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife Jenny is a person, weighing Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellectual soul, and Kantian dignity against Peter Singer's speciesism challenge to the person/animal moral line. They then argue walkers are 'impossible beings' like square-circles: Jenner's brain-stem-only reanimation cannot explain Hannah the bicycle girl crawling without organs, walkers smelling Rick in the rain, or cafeteria walkers moving for weeks without energy. On either the soul view or materialism walkers are not persons, so Morgan should shoot, and zombies fascinate because they are metaphysical projections of our fears, caught between being and nonbeing.

chapters.file: ch16 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
ch18 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Dave Beisecker takes AMC's 'stagger-on role' zombie contest as an amplified version of Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why relish playing a repulsive walker when zombification is the fate no rational creature would wish even on its remains? He rejects the curiosity solution through Nagel's bat—no staggering around a set could reveal what it is like to be a zombie, and we wouldn't survive zombification anyway except as our remains—and notes we fantasize about being survivors, not monsters. His answer is affection and release: walkers are the geeks and clowns of the undead pantheon, and playing one lets us comically own our inner loser, which is why Kirkman's symbol-free zombies invite identification where Nazi zombies would not.

chapters.file: ch19 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jason Walker pits Hobbes against Locke over whether Andrea may take the mermaid necklace when Rick says 'I don't think those rules apply anymore'. He reads the survivors' conduct—Andrea's single necklace under Locke's spoilage proviso, Morgan squatting in and fixing up the neighbors' house, Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo—as a Lockean state of nature where self-ownership and property rights persist without government, while Chris's cannibal band and the Governor embody the Hobbesian war of all against all, treating persons as mere means. The Lockean right to punish, exercised brutally by Grimes's group on Chris's hunters, vindicates rights even by Hobbes's own demand for enforcement.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Ashley Barkman argues feminism is unrealistic in a zombie apocalypse: citing Sax and Bandura on innate sex differences, she claims survival leadership demands masculine aggression and physical force, which is why Rick knocks Merle down and shoves off Daryl while no woman claims command in camp, farm, or Woodbury. She reads Jacqui's laundry protest as justified only against shirkers like Ed and Shane, not against Donna's complaint, since domestic work sustains morale, and concedes exceptional women—Andrea as the group's best shot, Michonne enduring the Governor's rape and enslavement and taking revenge. The conclusion is that roles, including the dangerous ones, should track natural difference rather than enforced equality.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Pye and O'Sullivan use Judith Butler's performativity to read walkers as genderless proof that gender is done, not born: the little-girl walker 'troubles' gender like drag, while survivors regressively re-perform patriarchy—Lori's 'I'm a girl, you talk to him', Carol at the washboard, the men confiscating Andrea's gun while Daryl keeps his crossbow. They invoke Butler's primitive clan and incest taboo to explain how Shane's camp, Lori and Carl's haircuts, and Ed's threats reproduce protector/protected roles, yet point to counterexamples—Andrea and Amy fishing, Felipe the nurse, Carl asking to be taught—that show roles can be learned differently. Via Rorty's remark that assumptions become visible when their contradictories sound plausible, they argue clinging to gender baggage endangers everyone against an enemy stripped of ego and social contract that does not discriminate.

chapters.file: ch22 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
ch23 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Rachel Robison-Greene applies Camus's absurdity to the series: walkers, like digger wasps, live meaningless loops without the self-reflective consciousness that 'poisons' experience, while survivors like Morgan longing for Jenny and Andrea for fishing trips with her father embody the clash between human longing and an indifferent universe, exactly as in Camus's The Plague at Oran. Suicide (Jacqui and Jenner as the CDC explodes) and religious consolation are escapist responses—the latter 'philosophical suicide'—so the authentic path is the absurd hero: Rick searching Atlanta for his family, Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side, the Vatos group caring for abandoned elders. Weighing Nagel's objection that absurdity arises from our clashing subjective and objective perspectives, she concludes we cheer Rick shooting Sophia in the barn because subjective commitment stays noble even where objective meaning is nowhere to be found.

chapters.file: ch24 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Si Sheppard reads the comic through Realist state-formation theory: Shane's leadership rests on borrowed prestige and dies with him, West Central Prison collapses into anarchy because Rick never establishes a monopoly on legitimate force—letting Tyreese's vigilante murder pass—nor any institution beyond his personal authority, while the Governor's Woodbury thrives on fear, arenas, and bread-and-circuses. Citing Machiavelli's prince who is feared rather than loved, Weber's definition of the state, and Bismarck's unifying wars, he argues the prison loses the 'second anarchy' rivalry with Woodbury for want of scouting, sabotage, coalition-building, or any command structure that survives Rick's absences. Rick's confession that he would kill everyone in the Alexandria Safe Zone to keep Lori safe is post-moral Realism, yet he was 'a bad founding father' who only finally learns to build an army instead of relying on himself.

holes.name: Functionalism (mental states as functional roles)
holes.what: The view that a mental state is defined by its causal role linking stimuli, other mental states, and behavior rather than by what a system is made of.
holes.why: Chapter 13 applies behaviorism and functionalism to walkers and refutes them with a walker-computer thought experiment adapted from Dennett, so a slug for the theory under test is needed.

holes.name: The Paradox of Horror
holes.what: Noel Carroll's puzzle of why audiences voluntarily seek out horror fiction whose monsters are engineered to provoke the negative emotions of fear and disgust.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames the desire to win a zombie extra role as an amplified paradox of horror and tests Carroll's curiosity-based solution before offering its own clownish-identification answer.

holes.name: Political Realism (power over morality)
holes.what: The theory that states exist to escape anarchy, that power rather than morality governs relations between them, and that security justifies otherwise immoral rule.
holes.why: Chapter 24 judges Rick's prison, Woodbury, and Alexandria entirely by Realist criteria drawn from Machiavelli, Weber, and Morgenthau, and no existing slug covers that framework.
